name: DJ Kool Herc
hook: Worked out that the few seconds dancers actually waited for could be made to last as long as he wanted, and built a form of music on that one idea.
blurb: Clive Campbell was born in Kingston and moved to the Bronx as a boy. At a back-to-school party his sister Cindy organised at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue on 11 August 1973, he did something simple and enormous: instead of playing a funk record through, he played the few seconds of drums that the dancers were waiting for, then cut to a second copy of the same record and played those seconds again. He called it the merry-go-round. The dancers who came alive during it got called break boys, b-boys. It made the break the unit music was built from, the idea sampling would later turn into an industry, and almost everything in hip-hop starts from it. He never released a record of his own, which makes him the clearest case on this map of an artist whose importance has nothing to do with a discography. Whether he brought Jamaican sound-system practice with him is genuinely disputed, and he has answered it both ways over decades of interviews. At times he has rejected any link to toasting outright, saying he could not play reggae to a Bronx crowd and naming James Brown and the Last Poets as the source of rap's vocal style. At other times he has described his DJing as something he brought from Jamaica. Scholars split the same way, some reading the likeness as shared African-American and Caribbean DJ roots rather than one passing it to the other. This map does not draw a line from Kingston to the Bronx, because the person it would run through says it is not there.
signatureTracksNote: Known for what he played at parties rather than for records of his own. The records he played are on his lines from James Brown and the Incredible Bongo Band.
